1. The Effect of Sample Size on Hypothesis Testing

children.label: 1. The Effect of Sample Size on Hypothesis Testing

children.value: We have already seen the effect that the sample size has on inference, when we discussed point and interval estimation for the population mean

children.html: (μ)(\mu)(μ)

children.value: Larger sample sizes give us more information to pin down the true nature of the population. We can therefore expect the

proportion obtained from a larger sample to be closer to the population mean and proportion, respectively. As a result, for the same level of confidence, we can report a smaller margin of error, and get a narrower confidence interval. What we’ve seen, then, is that a larger sample size gives a boost to how much we trust our sample results.

In hypothesis testing, larger sample sizes have a similar effect. The following two examples will illustrate that a larger sample size provides more convincing evidence, and how the evidence manifests itself in hypothesis testing. Let’s go back to our example 2 (marijuana use at a certain liberal arts college).

So far, nothing new. Let’s make small changes to the problem (and call it example 2*).
There are rumors that students in a certain liberal arts college are more inclined to use drugs than U.S. college students in general. Suppose that
in a simple random sample of 400 students from the college, 76 admitted to marijuana use
. Do the data provide enough evidence to conclude that the proportion of marijuana users among the students in the college (p) is
than the national proportion, which is 0.157?
We now have a larger sample (400 instead of 100), and we also changed the number of marijuana users (76 instead of 19). Let’s carry out the test in this case.
The question of interest did not change, so we are testing the same hypotheses:

What do we learn from these two examples?
We see that sample results that are based on a larger sample carry more weight.

In example 2, we saw that a sample proportion of 0.19 based on a sample of size 100 was not enough evidence that the proportion of marijuana users in the college is higher than 0.157. Recall, from our general overview of hypothesis testing, that this conclusion (not having enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis)
mean the null hypothesis is necessarily true (so we never “accept” the null); it only means that the particular study didn’t yield sufficient evidence to reject the null. It
be that the sample size was simply too small to detect a statistically significant difference.

However, in example 2*, we saw that when the sample proportion of 0.19 is obtained from a sample of size 400, it carries much more weight, and in particular, provides enough evidence that the proportion of marijuana users in the college is higher than 0.157 (the national figure). In
large enough to detect a statistically significant difference.
The following activity will allow you to practice the ideas and terminology used in hypothesis testing when a result is not statistically significant.
Suppose that only 40% of the U.S. public supported the general direction of the previous U.S. administration’s policies. To gauge whether the nationwide proportion, p, of support for the
administration is higher than 40%, a major polling organization conducts a random poll to test the hypotheses

model.question: Which is the correct interpretation of "not statistically significant" here?

choices.text: The poll did not provide enough evidence that support is higher than 40%
choices.feedback: Correct! The data do not provide enough evidence that support for the current administration exceeds 40%; we cannot reject $H_0$.

choices.text: The poll proved that support is exactly 40%
choices.feedback: Failing to reject $H_0$ does not prove that support equals 40%.

choices.text: The poll proved that support is NOT higher than 40%
choices.feedback: The poll may simply have been too small to detect a real difference—non-significance is not proof of no difference.

model.hint: What does a large p-value permit us to conclude—and not conclude?

model.question: Which of the following could explain the non-significant result?

choices.text: Either support truly is not above 40%, or the sample was too small to detect a real difference
choices.feedback: Correct! Either support truly isn't above 40%, or it is above 40% but the sample was too small to detect the difference—the test alone cannot tell us which.
This is only one of the possibilities—a real difference the study was too small to detect is also consistent with the result.

choices.text: Support is definitely above 40%, but the sample was too small
choices.feedback: This is also only one possibility—it could equally be that support truly is not higher than 40%.

model.hint: There are two possibilities: nothing is going on, or something is going on but the study missed it.

children.value: Now, we will address the issue of statistical significance versus practical importance (which also involves issues of sample size).
Check Your Understanding: Statistical vs. Practical Significance

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Statistical vs. Practical Significance

model.question: The result is highly statistically significant. Is it practically important?

choices.text: Probably not—a change from 10% to 10.05% is trivial, even though the huge sample makes it statistically significant
choices.feedback: Correct! With an enormous sample, even a trivial change (0.05 of a percentage point) becomes statistically significant. Statistical significance says the change is real, not that it matters.

choices.text: Yes—a p-value of 0.001 always indicates an important effect
choices.feedback: The p-value cannot measure the practical size of an effect—only the strength of evidence that some effect exists.

choices.text: The test must be invalid because the change is so small
choices.feedback: The significance is legitimate—the issue is that the underlying change is tiny.

model.hint: Look at the size of the change itself: from 10% to 10.05%.

model.question: What is the general lesson about very large samples in hypothesis testing?

choices.text: With very large samples, even tiny, unimportant differences become statistically significant—so always consider the effect size
choices.feedback: Correct! As n grows, the standard error shrinks, so even minuscule departures from the null value produce large test statistics and tiny p-values. Always ask whether the observed effect size is meaningful.

choices.text: Large samples make it harder to reach statistical significance
choices.feedback: Large samples make tests MORE sensitive, not less.

choices.text: Researchers should avoid collecting large samples
choices.feedback: Larger samples are generally better for estimation—the caution is about interpreting significance, not about avoiding large samples.

model.hint: Connect sample size, standard error, and what the test can "detect."
